input_signals.name: External finance funded investment intensity
input_signals.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(RATIO(ADD(capx, COALESCE(aqc, 0)), LAG(at, 1))), IND_RANK(RATIO(SUB(ADD(sstk, dltis), ADD(ADD(prstkc, dltr), dvc)), LAG(at, 1))))
input_signals.hypothesis: Firms whose total investment outlays (capex plus acquisitions) are simultaneously accompanied by large net external cash raising (equity plus debt issuance net of repurchases, debt retirement and dividends) are expanding beyond internal funding capacity, which signals overvaluation-driven timing and weak discipline; either channel alone is far less informative.
input_signals.reasoning: The product of the two industry-adjusted ranks is only large when heavy investment and heavy external funding co-occur, isolating externally funded expansion from self-funded investment. Netting out payouts ensures the financing leg measures true dependence on outside capital rather than gross issuance mechanics. Industry ranking removes sector-level capital intensity and issuance norms so the interaction is within-peer.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( ind_rank( ratio( add( capx, coalesce( aqc, 0 ) ), lag( at, 1 ) ) ), ind_rank( ratio( sub( add( sstk, dltis ), add( add( prstkc, dltr ), dvc ) ), lag( at, 1 ) ) ) )

input_signals.name: Sustained externally funded capacity buildout
input_signals.expression: MUL(RANK(TS_SUM(RATIO(SUB(ADD(sstk, dltis), ADD(prstkc, dltr)), at), 3)), RANK(GROWTH(ppegt, 3)))
input_signals.hypothesis: Multi-year, repeatedly financed physical capacity expansion reflects entrenched empire building rather than a one-off project, and such cumulative externally funded buildouts are followed by persistent disappointment in returns on capital.
input_signals.reasoning: Three-year cumulative net issuance paired with three-year gross PP&E growth captures a persistent state instead of a noisy annual flow, reducing the influence of single-year lumpy deals. The interaction separates firms that repeatedly tap markets to grow hard assets from firms that grew capacity out of internal cash flow. Longer windows should also stabilize portfolio composition and improve the reliability of the long-short alpha.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( rank( ts_sum( ratio( sub( add( sstk, dltis ), add( prstkc, dltr ) ), at ), 3 ) ), rank( growth( ppegt, 3 ) ) )

input_signals.name: Debt financed goodwill expansion
input_signals.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(DELTA(COALESCE(gdwl, 0), 1), LAG(at, 1))), RANK(RATIO(SUB(dltis, dltr), LAG(at, 1))))
input_signals.hypothesis: Growth in goodwill funded by net new long-term borrowing represents overpayment for targets levered onto the balance sheet, raising the probability of later impairments and financial distress, hence low future returns.
input_signals.reasoning: Goodwill growth is the accounting residue of premiums paid, and pairing it with net debt issuance identifies leveraged empire building rather than internally funded or stock-funded deals. The interaction differs from Signal 4 by isolating the debt-market channel, where creditor-supplied capital removes the equity-market discipline. Zero-filling missing goodwill is economically valid because absent goodwill means no acquired premium on the books.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( rank( ratio( delta( coalesce( gdwl, 0 ), 1 ), lag( at, 1 ) ) ), rank( ratio( sub( dltis, dltr ), lag( at, 1 ) ) ) )

input_signals.name: Financing raised in excess of investment parked in cash
input_signals.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(RATIO(SUB(SUB(ADD(sstk, dltis), ADD(prstkc, dltr)), ADD(capx, COALESCE(aqc, 0))), LAG(at, 1))), IND_RANK(RATIO(DELTA(che, 1), LAG(at, 1))))
input_signals.hypothesis: When a firm raises far more outside capital than its investment program absorbs and the surplus lands in cash, the issuance decision was driven by favorable market conditions (cheap equity/debt) rather than by investment opportunities; such supply-driven, project-less financing is followed by low returns as the mispricing corrects.
input_signals.reasoning: This replaces the hard indicator and the well-known equity-financed-asset-growth result with a continuous financing-investment wedge: both legs are ranked, so no mass of firms is pinned at zero and portfolio composition stays stable. The mechanism is the opposite of the accepted signals — here the diagnostic is external funding *without* matching real investment, verified by the concurrent cash build, which distinguishes opportunistic market timing from genuine project financing.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( ind_rank( ratio( sub( sub( add( sstk, dltis ), add( prstkc, dltr ) ), add( capx, coalesce( aqc, 0 ) ) ), lag( at, 1 ) ) ), ind_rank( ratio( delta( che, 1 ), lag( at, 1 ) ) ) )

input_signals.name: Dilutive real and intangible capital expansion
input_signals.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(RATIO(DELTA(ADD(ppegt, intan), 1), LAG(at, 1))), IND_RANK(GROWTH(csho, 1)))
input_signals.hypothesis: Expansion of the productive and intangible asset base that is accompanied by growth in the share count delivers little or no growth in capital per share, so the empire grows while shareholder claims are diluted; such expansion signals value-destroying scale-seeking and predicts low returns.
input_signals.reasoning: Using net share-count growth rather than sstk avoids the deal-event framing of the documented stock-financed-acquirer anomaly and measures actual net dilution after repurchases, while balance-sheet asset expansion avoids the arbitrary tied mass created by zero-filled aqc. The interaction is informative precisely because either leg alone is ambiguous: dilution funding no growth, or growth funded internally, are both far less diagnostic than growth whose per-share content is diluted away.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( ind_rank( ratio( delta( add( ppegt, intan ), 1 ), lag( at, 1 ) ) ), ind_rank( growth( csho, 1 ) ) )

input_signals.name: Chronic capital market dependence with heavy investment
input_signals.expression: SUMRANK(RATIO(ADD(capx, COALESCE(aqc, 0)), LAG(at, 1)), TS_SUM(INDICATOR(SUB(ADD(sstk, dltis), ADD(prstkc, dltr)), 0), 3))
input_signals.hypothesis: Firms that must tap external markets year after year to sustain a high investment rate have an investment program structurally beyond internal cash generation, and this chronic dependence — not any single financing event — is what predicts poor subsequent returns.
input_signals.reasoning: Counting the number of the last three years with positive net external financing converts a noisy annual flow into a habit state, which should cut portfolio turnover and stabilize the long-short composition that undermined the gen-0 alphas. It differs from the accepted three-year buildout signal by measuring financing *frequency* rather than cumulative magnitude, so a magnitude-versus-persistence comparison becomes possible.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: sumrank( ratio( add( capx, coalesce( aqc, 0 ) ), lag( at, 1 ) ), ts_sum( indicator( sub( add( sstk, dltis ), add( prstkc, dltr ) ), 0 ), 3 ) )

input_signals.name: Liability funded inventory buildup
input_signals.expression: SUMRANK(RATIO(DELTA(invt, 1), LAG(at, 1)), RATIO(DELTA(lt, 1), LAG(at, 1)))
input_signals.hypothesis: Inventory expansion financed by a growing liability stack reflects overestimated future demand plus no internal cash to absorb it; when sales disappoint, the firm faces markdowns while still owing creditors, so returns are low.
input_signals.reasoning: This moves the interaction from long-lived capital to working capital, a real-side channel absent from the archive, where the funding leg is the total claim stack rather than gross issuance flows and therefore captures accrued and trade financing as well as securities issuance. The mirror extreme — inventory liquidation with liabilities being paid down — is a coherent restructuring long leg rather than a residual mixture.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: sumrank( ratio( delta( invt, 1 ), lag( at, 1 ) ), ratio( delta( lt, 1 ), lag( at, 1 ) ) )

input_signals.name: Externally funded headcount expansion
input_signals.expression: SUMRANK(GROWTH(emp, 1), RATIO(SUB(ADD(sstk, dltis), ADD(prstkc, dltr)), LAG(at, 1)))
input_signals.hypothesis: Hiring sprees paid for with outside capital are the labor-side expression of empire building: headcount is a fixed, hard-to-reverse cost that managers add when capital is cheap, so externally funded workforce growth predicts subsequent margin disappointment and low returns.
input_signals.reasoning: Employment growth is a real-activity commitment that is not captured by capex, PP&E, or goodwill, so this tests whether the financing interaction generalizes across the type of resource being committed rather than being specific to balance-sheet capital. The long leg — shrinking headcount while retiring securities and debt — is a recognizable restructuring/discipline portfolio, keeping both tails interpretable.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: sumrank( growth( emp, 1 ), ratio( sub( add( sstk, dltis ), add( prstkc, dltr ) ), lag( at, 1 ) ) )

input_signals.name: Long lived investment on a debt refinancing treadmill
input_signals.expression: SUMRANK(RATIO(capx, LAG(ppegt, 1)), RATIO(ADD(dltis, dltr), LAG(at, 1)))
input_signals.hypothesis: Firms that sustain a high investment rate in long-lived productive assets while simultaneously running large gross debt issuance and repayment traffic are funding illiquid, long-duration projects with continuously rolled-over credit; this maturity and rollover mismatch makes their equity a levered claim on credit-market access rather than on project cash flow, so returns are low.
input_signals.reasoning: Unlike the archive's signals, the financing leg here is *gross* debt traffic (issuance plus retirement) rather than net external finance, so it measures refinancing dependence and rollover intensity — a channel invisible to net-issuance or share-count measures and not a repackaging of the published issuance or asset-growth anomalies. The capex rate is scaled by lagged gross PP&E so it measures replacement-plus-expansion intensity of the existing capital stack, and the opposite tail (low capex rate with quiet debt books) is a coherent, self-financed, low-rollover-risk long leg.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: sumrank( ratio( capx, lag( ppegt, 1 ) ), ratio( add( dltis, dltr ), lag( at, 1 ) ) )

input_signals.name: Investment weighted external funding intensity
input_signals.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(RATIO(ADD(capx, COALESCE(aqc, 0)), LAG(at, 1))), IND_ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(ADD(sstk, dltis), ADD(ADD(prstkc, dltr), dvc)), LAG(at, 1)), 1)))
input_signals.hypothesis: The return penalty attached to raising outside capital is proportional to how aggressively the firm is spending it on real investment: among heavy investors, net raisers of external capital are overvaluation-timers and empire builders while net returners of capital are demonstrably self-funded, and among firms that barely invest the funding mix carries little information.
input_signals.reasoning: This repairs the SIGN inconsistency by keeping the investment leg as a non-negative [0,1] intensity weight and the financing leg as a signed, winsorized, industry-centered z-score, so the signal is a genuine interaction slope: monotone in funding source conditional on investment, with low-investment firms shrinking toward zero rather than being pushed into either extreme. The short leg is therefore externally funded heavy investors and the long leg is self-funded heavy investors, which is the coherent two-sided portfolio the gen-0 rank-times-rank products could not form because both of their legs were non-negative.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( ind_rank( ratio( add( capx, coalesce( aqc, 0 ) ), lag( at, 1 ) ) ), ind_zscore( winsor( ratio( sub( add( sstk, dltis ), add( add( prstkc, dltr ), dvc ) ), lag( at, 1 ) ), 1 ) ) )

input_signals.name: Equity tilted funding of the investment program
input_signals.expression: SUMRANK(RATIO(ADD(capx, COALESCE(aqc, 0)), LAG(at, 1)), RATIO(sstk, ADD(sstk, dltis)))
input_signals.hypothesis: Among firms that do tap outside markets to invest, the choice of security is informative: equity-tilted funding signals that managers believe their shares are richly priced and escapes creditor scrutiny, while debt-tilted funding subjects the project to underwriting discipline and fixed repayment, so equity-funded investors underperform debt-funded investors with the same investment rate.
input_signals.reasoning: The financing leg is a bounded [0,1] composition share rather than a scaled magnitude, so it separates *which* market was used from *how much* was raised — a dimension no archived signal touches, and one that is orthogonal to the size of the investment program. Because the mix variable is not a growth or profitability characteristic, it should survive FF5 adjustment better than the net-flow magnitudes that CMA absorbed.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: sumrank( ratio( add( capx, coalesce( aqc, 0 ) ), lag( at, 1 ) ), ratio( sstk, add( sstk, dltis ) ) )

input_signals.name: Joint labor and dilution expansion conjunction
input_signals.expression: MIN(IND_RANK(GROWTH(emp, 1)), IND_RANK(GROWTH(csho, 1)))
input_signals.hypothesis: Empire building requires both a real commitment and outside money to pay for it; only firms that are simultaneously in the top of their industry on workforce growth and on share-count growth are expanding beyond internal capacity, and it is this conjunction — not either characteristic alone — that predicts low returns.
input_signals.reasoning: MIN is a Leontief conjunction rather than an additive blend, so a firm with heavy dilution but a shrinking workforce (or heavy hiring funded internally with no dilution) scores low — precisely the substitution that a SUMRANK could not prevent and that made the earlier version collapse onto the share-issuance leg. The high tail is therefore an economically specific "hire and dilute" portfolio, while the low tail is a broad diversified benchmark, which is the structure most likely to carry FF5 alpha given neither leg is spanned by CMA or RMW.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: min( ind_rank( growth( emp, 1 ) ), ind_rank( growth( csho, 1 ) ) )

input_signals.name: Soft asset buildout during abnormal own issuance
input_signals.expression: SUMRANK(RATIO(DELTA(COALESCE(intan, 0), 1), LAG(at, 1)), TS_RANK(RATIO(SUB(sstk, prstkc), at), 5))
input_signals.hypothesis: Purchased intangibles are the assets whose value outsiders can least verify, and managers finance them when their own equity is unusually expensive by their firm's own historical standards; abnormal-for-this-firm equity issuance funding soft-asset accumulation is the clearest overvaluation-exploitation combination and is followed by impairments and low returns.
input_signals.reasoning: The financing leg is replaced by a within-firm time-series percentile of asset-scaled net equity issuance, which removes the negative- and small-ceq explosion the critic identified and, more importantly, changes the economic content from "firms that issue a lot" (a cross-sectional type already in the archive) to "firms issuing unusually much for themselves" (a market-timing state). Because a firm-relative issuance rank is nearly orthogonal to persistent size, value, and investment loadings, it should be less absorbed by FF5 than the cross-sectional share-count level.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: sumrank( ratio( delta( coalesce( intan, 0 ), 1 ), lag( at, 1 ) ), ts_rank( ratio( sub( sstk, prstkc ), at ), 5 ) )

input_signals.name: Capital raised without a funding need
input_signals.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(RATIO(LAG(che, 1), LAG(at, 1))), IND_ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(ADD(sstk, dltis), ADD(prstkc, dltr)), LAG(at, 1)), 1)))
input_signals.hypothesis: Raising outside capital is only a warning sign when the firm did not need it: a cash-poor firm issues because projects require funding, whereas a firm that already sits on a large cash stock and still taps markets is exploiting favorable pricing or funding managerial ambition, and the same cash-rich firm that instead retires securities is signalling genuine discipline.
input_signals.reasoning: This replaces the additive cash-change leg — which the critic correctly noted contradicted the archived hoarding signal and so left issuance to dominate — with the *pre-existing cash stock as a conditioning weight* on signed financing, so the signal states when issuance is informative rather than adding a second anomaly. Firms with little cash shrink toward zero regardless of financing, the short tail is cash-rich raisers and the long tail is cash-rich returners of capital, giving two economically distinct extremes built from one interaction slope.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( ind_rank( ratio( lag( che, 1 ), lag( at, 1 ) ) ), ind_zscore( winsor( ratio( sub( add( sstk, dltis ), add( prstkc, dltr ) ), lag( at, 1 ) ), 1 ) ) )

input_signals.name: Borrowed money covering investment and dividends
input_signals.expression: WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(dltis, dltr), ADD(ADD(capx, COALESCE(aqc, 0)), dvc)), 1)
input_signals.hypothesis: Dividends are sticky commitments, so a firm that must borrow to cover its combined investment and payout obligations is running both a capital-expansion and a distribution promise it cannot internally fund; the fraction of these total commitments financed by net new debt measures the degree to which the firm's stated growth and payout policy is a credit-market construct.
input_signals.reasoning: This abandons the lagged-copy timing variant entirely and instead defines a new economic quantity — net debt raised per dollar of committed cash uses — whose denominator is a sum of non-negative flows, so there are no sign flips and the ratio is monotone in credit dependence. The mechanism (payout rigidity forcing leverage while investing) is absent from the archive, and because the denominator normalizes by the firm's own commitment scale rather than by assets, the measure is not a rescaled asset-growth variable that CMA would absorb.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: winsor( ratio( sub( dltis, dltr ), add( add( capx, coalesce( aqc, 0 ) ), dvc ) ), 1 )

input_signals.name: Investment under unstable external funding
input_signals.expression: SUMRANK(RATIO(ADD(capx, COALESCE(aqc, 0)), LAG(at, 1)), VOL(RATIO(SUB(ADD(sstk, dltis), ADD(prstkc, dltr)), at), 5))
input_signals.hypothesis: Firms that finance a large investment program out of an erratic, lumpy stream of outside capital have no reliable funding source, so their projects are hostage to windows of market receptivity; this funding fragility is a risk shareholders bear without compensation and predicts low returns.
input_signals.reasoning: Volatility of external financing is a second-moment channel absent from the archive and is conceptually distinct from both the level and the change of dependence — it captures unreliability rather than magnitude or surprise, so it should not inherit the sign inversion that afflicted the change-based legs. The five-year window costs some coverage, so the comparison against the level-based composites also tells us whether the alpha we have been earning is about funding reliability or funding quantity.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: sumrank( ratio( add( capx, coalesce( aqc, 0 ) ), lag( at, 1 ) ), vol( ratio( sub( add( sstk, dltis ), add( prstkc, dltr ) ), at ), 5 ) )

input_signals.name: Issuance despite cash covering the investment program
input_signals.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(WINSOR(RATIO(LAG(che, 1), ADD(capx, COALESCE(aqc, 0))), 1)), IND_ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(ADD(sstk, dltis), ADD(prstkc, dltr)), LAG(at, 1)), 1)))
input_signals.hypothesis: Outside funding is informative about managerial motive only when the firm had no need for it, and need is defined by cash on hand *relative to the size of the investment program*: a firm entering the year with cash covering several years of capital spending that still raises net outside capital is timing markets or funding ambition, while the same well-covered firm retiring securities is signalling discipline.
input_signals.reasoning: This repairs the critic's objection to the bounded-NEF ratio — investment no longer enters as a mere scale factor but defines the funding-need benchmark in the conditioning weight, so the interaction is intrinsic rather than cosmetic. It also sharpens the archive's strongest joint result (cash/assets × signed financing, alpha −3.3%, t −3.19) by replacing an asset-scaled cash ratio with a coverage-of-investment ratio, which is the economically correct measure of whether the raise was necessary.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( ind_rank( winsor( ratio( lag( che, 1 ), add( capx, coalesce( aqc, 0 ) ) ), 1 ) ), ind_zscore( winsor( ratio( sub( add( sstk, dltis ), add( prstkc, dltr ) ), lag( at, 1 ) ), 1 ) ) )

input_signals.name: Capacity expansion funded by firm abnormal dilution
input_signals.expression: MIN(IND_RANK(RATIO(DELTA(ppegt, 1), LAG(at, 1))), TS_RANK(GROWTH(csho, 1), 5))
input_signals.hypothesis: Managers expand physical capacity while diluting shareholders at a rate unusually high by their own firm's standards; the firm-relative abnormality identifies the timing decision, whereas a high cross-sectional issuance level mostly identifies a persistent firm type that the market already prices.
input_signals.reasoning: This drops the mis-specified equity-share denominator (where repurchasers were labelled debt funded) and replaces the cross-sectional dilution level — whose archived level version produced contrary positive alpha — with a within-firm time-series percentile, the specification that delivered sign-consistent alpha for the soft-asset signal. The MIN conjunction ensures the high tail is specifically "expanding *and* diluting abnormally," so neither leg can substitute for the other.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: min( ind_rank( ratio( delta( ppegt, 1 ), lag( at, 1 ) ) ), ts_rank( growth( csho, 1 ), 5 ) )

input_signals.name: Market funded share of all cash uses
input_signals.expression: WINSOR(RATIO(ADD(sstk, dltis), ADD(ADD(capx, COALESCE(aqc, 0)), ADD(ADD(dvc, prstkc), dltr))), 1)
input_signals.hypothesis: Every dollar a firm deploys — capital expenditure, acquisitions, dividends, buybacks, debt repayment — is funded either from operations or from the capital market, so gross funds raised divided by total cash uses measures the market-funded share directly, and its complement is the internally funded share; high market-funded share identifies expansion the firm cannot support from within.
input_signals.reasoning: This answers the critique that internal funding was only inferred: the denominator is the firm's complete set of cash uses and the numerator its gross external sources, so the ratio measures the funding split explicitly through the sources-equals-uses identity rather than by assumption. All components are non-negative flows and the denominator is positive for essentially every firm, so unlike the earlier deficit ratios there are no sign flips, no issuer-only sample restriction, and no reliance on a positive-sign long tail that the investment anomaly would fight.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: winsor( ratio( add( sstk, dltis ), add( add( capx, coalesce( aqc, 0 ) ), add( add( dvc, prstkc ), dltr ) ) ), 1 )

input_signals.name: Unneeded equity issuance by liquid firms
input_signals.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(RATIO(LAG(che, 1), LAG(at, 1))), IND_ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(sstk, prstkc), LAG(at, 1)), 1)))
input_signals.hypothesis: Selling shares while sitting on ample cash is the sharpest possible statement that management considers its equity expensive, since no funding shortfall can justify the dilution; conversely, a cash-rich firm repurchasing shares is acting on the belief that its equity is cheap.
input_signals.reasoning: This is the equity counterpart to Signal 2 and completes the attribution of the archive's strongest result to a specific market, using the identical conditioning weight and scaling so the comparison is interpretable. It also supersedes the gen-3 equity-dependence test, which was confounded by using an additive combiner and a first difference at the same time (alpha only −0.8%).
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( ind_rank( ratio( lag( che, 1 ), lag( at, 1 ) ) ), ind_zscore( winsor( ratio( sub( sstk, prstkc ), lag( at, 1 ) ), 1 ) ) )

input_signals.name: Liquid heavy investors raising more capital
input_signals.expression: MUL(MIN(IND_RANK(RATIO(LAG(che, 1), LAG(at, 1))), IND_RANK(RATIO(ADD(capx, COALESCE(aqc, 0)), LAG(at, 1)))), IND_ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(ADD(sstk, dltis), ADD(prstkc, dltr)), LAG(at, 1)), 1)))
input_signals.hypothesis: The penalty for unneeded capital raising should be concentrated among firms that are actually spending aggressively — cash-rich, heavily investing firms that still tap markets are the true empire builders — whereas cash-rich firms that raise money and invest little are merely hoarding and face a smaller correction.
input_signals.reasoning: The conditioning weight becomes the conjunction of liquidity and investment intensity, so this tests directly whether the archive's cash-conditioned result is an overinvestment phenomenon or a pure market-timing phenomenon — an economically decisive question that the single-conditioner versions cannot answer. Using MIN prevents a very high investment rate from substituting for liquidity, keeping the high-weight group narrowly defined as liquid expanders.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( min( ind_rank( ratio( lag( che, 1 ), lag( at, 1 ) ) ), ind_rank( ratio( add( capx, coalesce( aqc, 0 ) ), lag( at, 1 ) ) ) ), ind_zscore( winsor( ratio( sub( add( sstk, dltis ), add( prstkc, dltr ) ), lag( at, 1 ) ), 1 ) ) )

input_signals.name: Raising capital while distributing internal surplus
input_signals.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(WINSOR(RATIO(dvc, ADD(capx, COALESCE(aqc, 0))), 1)), IND_ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(ADD(sstk, dltis), ADD(prstkc, dltr)), LAG(at, 1)), 1)))
input_signals.hypothesis: A firm that pays out substantial dividends relative to the size of its investment program has revealed, through its own committed cash flow, that internal resources exceed its spending needs; when such a firm simultaneously raises net outside capital it is round-tripping capital — taking money in at one window while handing it out at another — which signals timing or agency motives rather than financing a shortfall.
input_signals.reasoning: This replaces the smoothed cash-stock conditioner (a turnover variant) with an economically different definition of "no funding need": revealed internal capacity from a committed distribution flow benchmarked against the investment program, rather than a liquidity stock on the balance sheet. Because the weight is a payout-to-investment ratio, non-payers receive zero weight and sit in the middle, so the extremes are dividend-paying capital raisers versus dividend-paying capital retirers — two sharply interpretable portfolios that do not depend on the cash-richness dimension already tested in the archive.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( ind_rank( winsor( ratio( dvc, add( capx, coalesce( aqc, 0 ) ) ), 1 ) ), ind_zscore( winsor( ratio( sub( add( sstk, dltis ), add( prstkc, dltr ) ), lag( at, 1 ) ), 1 ) ) )

input_signals.name: Equity issued despite unused debt capacity
input_signals.expression: MUL(MIN(IND_RANK(NEG(RATIO(LAG(lt, 1), LAG(at, 1)))), IND_RANK(RATIO(capx, LAG(at, 1)))), IND_ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(sstk, prstkc), LAG(at, 1)), 1)))
input_signals.hypothesis: Pecking order implies that an investing firm with a light claim stack should exhaust cheap debt before selling equity, so choosing equity while borrowing capacity sits unused reveals that management regards its shares as overpriced; the same low-leverage investor repurchasing shares reveals the opposite belief and should outperform.
input_signals.reasoning: The motivation is corrected: the archive contains no test of the low-leverage pole — the gen-3 stretched-claim-stack signal was insignificant (fmb −0.39) and exploited the opposite end of the leverage dimension, so this signal is an untested state, justified by pecking-order theory rather than by that result. Its only support from the archive is structural, namely that a non-negative predetermined conditioning weight multiplied by a signed, centered financing intensity is the one form that has produced sign-consistent alpha (−3.3% and −2.7%), and the investment leg is deliberately restricted to organic capex because acquisitions often require stock as deal currency, which would contaminate a test about voluntary security choice.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( min( ind_rank( neg( ratio( lag( lt, 1 ), lag( at, 1 ) ) ) ), ind_rank( ratio( capx, lag( at, 1 ) ) ) ), ind_zscore( winsor( ratio( sub( sstk, prstkc ), lag( at, 1 ) ), 1 ) ) )

input_signals.name: Net financial slack conditioning of capital raising
input_signals.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(RATIO(SUB(LAG(che, 1), LAG(lt, 1)), LAG(at, 1))), IND_ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(ADD(sstk, dltis), ADD(prstkc, dltr)), LAG(at, 1)), 1)))
input_signals.hypothesis: Gross cash overstates freedom from funding need because a firm can hold a large cash balance against even larger obligations; true slack is cash net of the claims already outstanding, and it is firms with genuinely unencumbered resources that have no excuse for tapping markets, while the same unencumbered firms retiring securities are the clearest self-funded type.
input_signals.reasoning: This changes the economic definition of the conditioner rather than smoothing it: netting liabilities against cash separates cash-rich-but-levered firms (whose raises may be genuine refinancing) from firms with real surplus, which should sharpen both tails of the winning structure. input_signals.hypothesis: Conditional on already being liquid, the informative quantity is the share of the firm's capital deployment that comes from outside rather than the dollar size of the raise: a liquid firm whose spending is overwhelmingly market-funded is timing or empire building, while a liquid firm spending its own money and retiring securities is self-funding.

input_signals.hypothesis: A liquid firm that raises money in the equity market and the debt market in the same year is displaying funding hunger that no shortfall explains, since either market alone would have covered a genuine need; conversely a liquid firm that is materially retiring claims in at least one market is returning capital rather than accumulating it.
input_signals.reasoning: Rather than crossing two evaluated parents, this exploits the specific puzzle they created — the equity leg carried the cross-sectional slope (fmb −5.22) while the debt leg carried the alpha (t −2.12) with almost no slope — by asking whether the two channels are complements, using MIN so that neither can substitute for the other. The construction is not collinear with either parent because simultaneous issuers are a small, distinct subset, and firms that issue equity while deleveraging (or borrow while repurchasing) are pushed to the middle rather than the short tail, which sharpens the identification of pure capital accumulation.

input_signals.hypothesis: Outside funding is not confined to securities markets — payables, accruals and other non-financial obligations also finance expansion — so a liquid firm that grows its entire stack of outside claims is drawing on suppliers and counterparties as well as investors, and the same liquid firm shrinking its claim stack is retreating to self-funding.
input_signals.reasoning: This is a scope test of the mechanism: if the penalty attaches to unneeded outside funding in general, total-liability growth under liquidity should predict returns much like security issuance does; if only securities markets matter, the mechanism is specifically about investor mispricing rather than about resource accumulation. The liability change is dense and does not require cash-flow-statement items, so coverage should be at the top of the archive's range, giving a well-powered comparison.

input_signals.hypothesis: A single year in which a liquid firm draws on both shareholders and creditors can be lumpy timing, but a firm that has accumulated capital from both markets in every year of a three-year window has institutionalized market dependence despite holding ample cash — a standing state of funding hunger that resolves into poor returns as the accumulated capital fails to earn its cost.

input_signals.name: Equity issuance by collateral rich firms
input_signals.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(RATIO(LAG(ppent, 1), LAG(at, 1))), IND_ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(sstk, prstkc), LAG(at, 1)), 1)))

input_signals.reasoning: The conditioner is asset collateralizability — a real, predetermined property of the investment stock — rather than another point on the liquidity/leverage continuum already bracketed by gross cash, cash minus liabilities, and the lagged liability ratio, so it tests a different reason why a raise is unnecessary. It also predicts a sharp asymmetry the archive cannot produce: the same equity issuance should be uninformative among intangible-intensive firms and strongly negative among tangible-asset firms, with the long tail being collateral-rich repurchasers.

input_signals.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(RATIO(LAG(ppent, 1), LAG(ppegt, 1))), IND_ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(ADD(sstk, dltis), ADD(prstkc, dltr)), LAG(at, 1)), 1)))
input_signals.hypothesis: The ratio of net to gross plant measures how much of the existing capital stock is still unamortized, so a high value means the firm has recently built capacity that has not yet been through a full earnings cycle; raising fresh outside capital in that state means doubling down before the last vintage has proven itself, whereas firms with a fully depreciated base that are retiring securities are harvesting mature assets.
input_signals.reasoning: This replaces the collinear liquidity blend with a conditioning state the archive has never used — the vintage of installed capacity, which is a property of the investment stock rather than of the balance-sheet liquidity or collateral dimensions already tested (the collateral test used ppent/at, a very different construct dominated by industry asset mix). The economic content is serial, unproven expansion, so a negative result here separates "raising when unproven capacity is already on the ground" from the pure market-timing reading supported by the liquidity conditioner.

input_signals.hypothesis: Independent of how many dollars move, the direction of a firm's capital-market activity is informative: a liquid firm whose securities traffic is nearly all intake has adopted an accumulating posture, while a liquid firm whose traffic is nearly all repurchase and repayment has adopted a returning posture, and posture predicts returns even for firms whose net flow is modest.
input_signals.reasoning: Every archive financing leg has measured *magnitude* of net flow scaled by assets, so small-but-purely-accumulating firms and large offsetting firms have been conflated; the intake share of total gross traffic is bounded in [0,1], defined for any firm with any capital-market activity, and isolates direction from size. This is a substantively different construct rather than a pre- versus post-standardization reordering of the previously tested dual-channel conjunction.

input_signals.hypothesis: What a firm takes in from investors is a decision distinct from what it hands back, so netting the two destroys information: a liquid firm taking in large gross proceeds is accumulating outside capital it does not need even if it simultaneously repays maturing debt, while a liquid firm with essentially no intake is genuinely self-funding.
input_signals.reasoning: This drops the share-count proxy the critic identified as a restatement of composite issuance and instead tests the gross-versus-net decomposition of the winning financing leg, an accounting distinction with a real economic claim — simultaneous repayment is often contractual rather than discretionary and should not be allowed to offset discretionary intake. Together with Signal 2 it decomposes the archive's net-flow measure into magnitude of intake and direction of posture, so the pair tells the final generation which component of net external financing the liquidity conditioner is actually pricing.

input_signals.hypothesis: A firm whose gross productive capacity is shrinking has no growth program to finance, so outside capital raised in that state is funding losses, legacy obligations or working-capital gaps rather than investment; conversely a firm shrinking its capacity while retiring securities is executing a genuine, self-funded contraction.

If the shrinking-capacity state gives a larger alpha, the mechanism is about financing decline rather than about market timing by comfortable firms.

input_signals.hypothesis: Goodwill on the balance sheet is the accumulated record of premiums a management team has paid for other companies, so a large goodwill stock identifies a habitual acquirer; when such a firm returns to capital markets for more funding, it is refilling the tank of a demonstrated empire builder whose past purchases are candidates for impairment.

input_signals.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(GROWTH(emp, 1)), IND_ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(ADD(sstk, dltis), ADD(prstkc, dltr)), LAG(at, 1)), 1)))
input_signals.hypothesis: Headcount is the least reversible commitment a firm can make — far stickier than capex, which can be halted — so a hiring surge paid for with outside capital locks in a cost base that the market's money, not the firm's cash flow, is supporting, and margins disappoint when the funding window closes; firms cutting headcount while retiring securities are the disciplined opposite.
